quotes: GitHub attributes a commit to an account by matching the email address in the commit with the addresses on accounts (why are my commits linked to the wrong user). The avatar and the profile link beside a commit are therefore a lookup of a string that the committer chose. Anyone with push access can make a commit display as a colleague, or as any public figure whose email is known (demonstration).

slides.body: This is a defensive video. You need to see how little it takes, so that you stop trusting the author line and know what to trust instead.
Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.
First, identity without signatures: the author and committer lines are assertions, and neither Git nor a push checks them.
The scripts signature-scope and spoof-signed generate fresh keys, so they're volatile: your IDs and key fingerprints differ from the ones on screen.
Here's what you'll walk away with.

slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Treating the author line or git shortlog as evidence of who made a commit. Root cause: author and committer are text supplied by whoever creates the commit.
Treating exit status 0 of git verify-commit as "the author signed this". Root cause: Git verifies the signature against the trusted keys and never compares the signer with the author line.
Relying on git merge --verify-signatures as a history policy. Root cause: it verifies only the tip commit of the side branch.
Removing an old key from the allowed-signers file at rotation. Root cause: verification looks the key up in the file, so old commits turn from G to U; rotation adds, never replaces.
Expecting signatures to survive a rebase, a squash or a history filter. Root cause: a rewrite writes new objects, signed by the operator's key or by none.

slides.lead: You should now be able to say:
items: Author and committer are assertions; Git and the push check them against nothing, and a plain Git server accepts a forged author.
A signature covers every byte of one object and nothing outside it: not refs, not the push, not later rewrites.
Amend, rebase and cherry-pick write new commits, signed by the operator or not at all.
git verify-commit answers "did a trusted key sign this", not "did the named author sign this"; comparing signer and author is a policy you run yourself.
git merge --verify-signatures checks only the tip.

Third, the forgery again in a repository where everyone signs, and the difference between verifying a signature and enforcing a policy.

beats.text: Identity. In one sentence: the author and committer of a commit are two lines of text that the person running Git supplies, and neither Git nor a push checks them against anything.
beats.tele: Identity. In one sentence: the author and committer of a commit are two lines of text that the person running Git supplies, and neither Git nor a push checks them against anything.

beats.text: Precisely. git commit takes the author from the environment variables GIT_AUTHOR_NAME and GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL, or from --author, or from user.name and user.email. It takes the committer from the GIT_COMMITTER variables or the same configuration. Those strings become the author and committer headers of the commit object and are covered by the commit ID.
beats.tele: Precisely. `git commit` takes the author from the environment variables `GIT_AUTHOR_NAME` and `GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL`, or from `--author`, or from `user.name` and `user.email`. It takes the committer from the `GIT_COMMITTER` variables or the same configuration. Those strings become the `author` and `committer` headers of the commit object and are covered by the commit ID.

beats.text: The transport authenticates the pusher. It doesn't compare the pusher with the names inside the commits being pushed, and the textbook adds that it couldn't: pushing other people's commits is what a merge, a rebase and a cherry-pick do every day. There's no bug here to fix. The design requires it.

There's no bug here to fix. The design requires it.

beats.text: Not every use of another person's name is a forgery. --author changes one field and leaves you as committer, which is how a patch from someone else is honestly recorded. The forgery is the claim of both fields, and to Git the two cases are the same operation.
beats.tele: Not every use of another person's name is a forgery. `--author` changes one field and leaves you as committer, which is how a patch from someone else is honestly recorded. The forgery is the claim of both fields, and to Git the two cases are the same operation.

says: --author changes one field. A forgery claims both. To Git it is the same operation

beats.text: What a signature covers. Everything in the object. Tree, parents, author, committer, dates and message are all signed bytes. Through the tree and parent IDs, a signature vouches for every file and every ancestor.
beats.tele: What a signature covers. Everything in the object. Tree, parents, author, committer, dates and message are all signed bytes. Through the tree and parent IDs, a signature vouches for every file and every ancestor.

beats.text: What it does not cover. Nothing outside the object. Three things matter most.
beats.tele: What it does not cover. Nothing outside the object. Three things matter most.

beats.text: Refs aren't signed. A ref is a name, such as a branch or a tag, that points at an object. Which branch or tag name points at the object isn't part of the object. A signed commit stays validly signed on any branch, in any repository. Anyone who can push can serve your signed tag object under another name. The object still says its original tag name inside, which is why a careful verifier compares that name with the one it asked for.
beats.tele: Refs aren't signed. A ref is a name, such as a branch or a tag, that points at an object. Which branch or tag name points at the object isn't part of the object. A signed commit stays validly signed on any branch, in any repository. Anyone who can push can serve your signed tag object under another name. The object still says its original tag name inside, which is why a careful verifier compares that name with the one it asked for.

beats.text: Quick quiz. A colleague rebases your two signed commits, and signs while doing it. Whose key is on the new commits? A, yours. B, theirs. Your answer?
beats.tele: Quick quiz. A colleague rebases your two signed commits, and signs while doing it. Whose key is on the new commits? A, yours. B, theirs. Your answer?

beats.text: B, theirs. Rewrites aren't covered. Amend, rebase and cherry-pick, three commands that replace or copy commits, write new commits. The new commits are signed only if the person running the command signs, and then with their key, not the original author's.
beats.tele: B, theirs. Rewrites aren't covered. Amend, rebase and cherry-pick, three commands that replace or copy commits, write new commits. The new commits are signed only if the person running the command signs, and then with their key, not the original author's.

beats.text: The push isn't covered. Who pushed is known only to the server's logs.
beats.tele: The push isn't covered. Who pushed is known only to the server's logs.

beats.text: Key lifetime and revocation. An allowed-signers entry can carry valid-after and valid-before. Git passes the committer date of the object as the time to check against. And the committer date is whatever the committer says. So validity windows let you rotate keys without invalidating old signatures, which is what the manual offers them for. They don't protect against a stolen key, because the thief chooses the date.
beats.tele: Key lifetime and revocation. An allowed-signers entry can carry `valid-after` and `valid-before`. Git passes the committer date of the object as the time to check against. And the committer date is whatever the committer says. So validity windows let you rotate keys without invalidating old signatures, which is what the manual offers them for. They don't protect against a stolen key, because the thief chooses the date.

beats.text: For a stolen key there's the revocation file, gpg.ssh.revocationFile. A revoked key fails for every date, including all the honest signatures made before the theft. That's the price.
beats.tele: For a stolen key there's the revocation file, `gpg.ssh.revocationFile`. A revoked key fails for every date, including all the honest signatures made before the theft. That's the price.

beats.text: Verification is not policy. git verify-commit verifies a signature against the list of trusted keys. It doesn't compare the signer with the author line. That comparison is a policy, and you have to run it. And git merge --verify-signatures isn't that policy either: the manual says it verifies "the tip commit of the side branch". One commit.

That comparison is a policy, and you have to run it. And `git merge --verify-signatures` isn't that policy either: the manual says it verifies "the tip commit of the side branch". One commit.

beats.text: When not to rely on it. From section 14B.20: a signature is evidence about a key. A passphrase-less key on a laptop, a key copied into CI, or a shared team key reduce "signed by Asha" to "signed by something that had Asha's file".

beats.text: Analogy, from section 21B.5. The author line is the return address on an envelope. The postal service delivers the letter whatever you write there. A signature is the wax seal: it proves which seal pressed the wax, and it still says nothing about what the letter asks you to do.
beats.tele: Analogy, from section 21B.5. The author line is the return address on an envelope. The postal service delivers the letter whatever you write there. A signature is the wax seal: it proves which seal pressed the wax, and it still says nothing about what the letter asks you to do.

beats.text: Where it breaks: a wax seal sits on the outside and you can look at it without opening anything. A Git signature is inside the object and covers the return address too. So a signed commit does protect its author line against later change by a third party. What it can't do is make the author line true at the moment of signing. The signer wrote both.

beats.text: If the commit is unsigned, Git can't say who made it. The honest answer is "anyone with push access", and the investigation goes to the server's record of who pushed. If the commit is signed, Git can say which key signed it: run the log with %G?, the author address and %GS. If the signer isn't the author, you have a named key and its owner to talk to. Section 14B.19 says how to treat a signed history that contains a commit its named author never made: as an incident.
